video_title: MacroVoices #542 Luke Gromen: As The Conflict Turns
gist: Forest for the Trees founder Luke Gromen (transcribed variably as 'Groman'/'Roman') tells Erik Townsend that China's demonstrated ability to absorb oil-demand pain gives it the geopolitical upper hand in prolonging the Iran conflict, which he ties to a broader Hamiltonian-economics/gold-settlement endgame for US policy and a coming sovereign bond crisis; the episode closes with a Macro Voices Trading Desk segment laying out a specific GLD options trade and current COT positioning across equities, currencies, oil, gold and copper.

insights.claim: In the first half of 2026 China shifted about 1.4 million barrels per day of oil demand to EVs and cut overall oil demand by 3-4 million barrels per day, while its exports to the world rose 27% year-over-year in May and corporate profits rose 19-20% year-to-date, showing it absorbed the Iran-conflict shock far better than consensus expected.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Demonstrates China has real, usable slack to manage global oil supply shocks, undercutting the consensus view that China would be the biggest loser from a prolonged Middle East conflict.

insights.claim: China's incentive is to keep oil prices 'low enough to not create a severe crisis, high enough to keep inflation elevated' in the West while selling weapons and components to all sides of ongoing conflicts, because a prolonged US war economy structurally benefits China's relative position, just as the 23-year Iraq/Afghanistan war era did.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Implies markets should expect China to be a stabilizing-but-not-resolving actor on oil prices for as long as it serves Beijing's strategic interest, capping downside but not necessarily preventing renewed spikes.
insights.quote: The longer the US stays at war, the better it is for them.

insights.claim: Solar power generation in Asia has now overtaken gas generation, evidence that Chinese-subsidized solar panels, EVs, and battery arrays are structurally reducing regional oil (and by extension dollar) demand across the global south.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A structural, non-cyclical drag on long-run oil demand growth from emerging Asia, relevant to long-horizon energy-demand and de-dollarization forecasts.

insights.claim: Yuan trade volumes on China's CIPS (Cross-Border Interbank Payment System) hit an all-time record in May at roughly 14 trillion yuan (about $2 trillion) for the month, signaling accelerating use of yuan settlement outside the dollar system.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable metric for monitoring the pace of de-dollarization in global trade settlement.

insights.claim: China's new helium export ban - announced even though helium prices are near multi-year lows - is read by Gromen as a signpost that China expects the conflict to extend and is pre-positioning against a possible US retaliatory cutoff of helium, a critical input for semiconductor manufacturing (the US and Qatar are the top two producers).
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: An unusual, easily overlooked commodity-policy signal worth tracking as a leading indicator of both conflict duration and US-China chip-supply-chain tensions.

insights.claim: Gromen cites a viral Kishore Mahbubani speech arguing 'the west is sleepwalking into its downfall' and notes rest-of-world sentiment often rates China more favorably than the US, referencing Larry Summers' line that 'when the Americans come, we get a lecture, when the Chinese come, we get an airport.'
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Frames a soft-power dimension to the US-China contest that could shape which currency/trade bloc developing-world partners gravitate toward over time.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz has remained closed far longer than consensus expected - still closed as of July 21 - vindicating Gromen's earlier call, but the oil-price and inflation spike he and Townsend both expected did not fully materialize because of China's aggressive demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A confirmed, dated geopolitical call (Hormuz closure duration) with an acknowledged miss on price magnitude, useful for calibrating how much weight to give Gromen's other active calls.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent effectively forced a de-grossing of speculative leverage in the oil market during the March-April volatility spike (MOVE index near dysfunctional levels on March 27), preventing a disorderly price blowout even as physical constraints (SPR drawdowns, Houthi attacks disrupting the Red Sea reroute) remain unresolved.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Credits deliberate policy/market intervention (not just fundamentals) for suppressing oil volatility, implying that once leverage rebuilds the market could be vulnerable to a sharper repricing.

insights.claim: Gromen says oil's near-term direction is now 'too hard' to call with conviction given how many swing factors are in play (China's willingness to intervene, SPR depletion, Houthi disruption of the Red Sea reroute), so he owns gold instead as a lower-volatility proxy that he expects to at least keep pace with oil.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A pragmatic 'too hard, own gold instead' framework for investors who find direct oil positioning too binary/event-driven right now.

insights.claim: Erik Townsend raises the scenario that China could keep suppressing oil prices as an implicit favor to Trump ahead of elections, but could instead let prices run toward $200 if it decides not to extend that favor, framing oil's range as genuinely bimodal ($50 vs. $200) rather than a single consensus forecast.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Highlights China's oil-price lever as a live political variable tied to the US election calendar, an underappreciated source of near-term oil-price tail risk in both directions.

themes.theme: US Fiscal Endgame: Hamiltonian Economics & Gold

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent and US Trade Representative Greer have both explicitly invoked 'Hamiltonian economics' - high tariffs plus a neutral reserve asset - as the administration's monetary strategy, which Gromen interprets as an implicit embrace of gold (not the yuan) as the intended neutral settlement asset, aligning with China's own long-stated 20-year goal of a gold-settled, non-credit-based reserve system.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: If accurate, this is a structural, policy-level bullish gold thesis independent of near-term crisis trading, since it implies the US and China are converging on gold as reserve-system infrastructure.
insights.quote: the US is moving to Hamiltonian economics

insights.claim: Gold has been the US's number-one export by value in eight of the last ten months, ahead of pharmaceutical preparations, jet engines, and oil (with oil and pharma taking the top spot in the other two months).
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A striking, underreported data point on gold's growing role in US trade flows that supports the broader gold-as-reserve-asset thesis.
insights.quote: in the last 10 months, eight of those 10 months, gold has been the US's number one export. Bigger than pharmaceutical preparations, bigger than jet engines, bigger than oil.

insights.claim: Gromen predicts every major sovereign bond market (US, Japan, Europe, UK, Korea) is 'straining on the upside' except China's, and expects one of them to break first and force some form of explicit or implicit yield curve control, after which the others would need to follow.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A specific, high-conviction global bond-crisis call; investors should watch for the first G7/Korea sovereign bond market to show acute stress as the trigger event.

insights.claim: If yield curve control is triggered somewhere, Gromen expects the affected currencies to weaken together against gold and the yuan, local-currency equity markets to rise nominally but fall in gold terms, and gold and Bitcoin to both perform well as the beneficiaries of the resulting financial repression.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Lays out a specific multi-asset playbook (long gold, long Bitcoin, short local-currency real equity returns) for a coordinated developed-market currency-debasement scenario.

insights.claim: Japan, Germany, and Korea - historically the world's largest creditor/surplus nations - are now simultaneously pivoting to become net borrowers to fund 'defense stimmies' (fiscal stimulus for rearmament), which Gromen sees as structurally inflationary since defense-industrial reshoring largely excludes China, the world's largest defense-industrial base.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A notable regime change - the world's traditional bond buyers becoming bond sellers/issuers - with direct inflationary and rate implications across DM sovereign curves.

insights.claim: In the week of the interview, markets showed a rare simultaneous 'war on, rates up, oil up, gold up' pattern - a reversal of the prior five months' pattern where war escalation had pushed gold down - which Gromen reads as the start of markets pricing longer-term inflation and financial-repression consequences rather than short-term liquidation.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A potential regime-change signal in cross-asset correlations worth confirming over subsequent weeks before treating it as a durable trend.

themes.theme: AI Race: China vs US Semiconductors

insights.claim: Gromen sees the current moment as the AI-industry version of a 25-year pattern he witnessed in US industrials versus China: 'cheaper but worse' becomes 'cheaper and about as good' becomes 'cheaper and better' - and argues Chinese AI models have now credibly crossed into the 'better and cheaper' phase, a shift markets are underpricing given how many times this pattern has repeated in other sectors.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Challenges the assumption of durable US AI-model superiority, a key risk factor for valuations of US frontier AI labs and related equities.

insights.claim: A Chinese AI firm (Z.AI) is reported running a roughly 1-gigawatt data center entirely on Chinese-made semiconductors with no Nvidia hardware, which Gromen views as early proof that 2022 US chip-export controls are backfiring by accelerating Chinese chip self-sufficiency, with a 'cheaper and better' Chinese chip stack plausible within about five years.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A concrete data point supporting a bear case on long-run Nvidia/US-semiconductor competitive moat tied specifically to China's addressable market and domestic substitution.

insights.claim: Gromen recommends a Substack essay (by a writer using the handle 'groundbreaker', published in early July, before the recent Chinese-model selloff in semis) arguing AI hyperscalers should be analyzed like real-estate/credit companies, where the real risk isn't falling demand but the second derivative of growth slowing enough that heavy debt can't be refinanced against a falling asset value.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Offers a specific analytical lens (real-estate/credit-refinancing risk, not simple demand risk) for stress-testing AI-infrastructure and hyperscaler valuations.

insights.claim: Gromen's near-term view is that if the US AI narrative cracks, semiconductor stocks get dragged down as collateral damage, which he would treat as a buying opportunity because he still expects the US-China AI capex race to ultimately lift semiconductor demand over a multi-year horizon.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A tactical buy-the-dip framework on semiconductors specifically tied to any AI-narrative-driven selloff, distinct from a structural bearish call on the sector.

insights.claim: Gromen remains highly positioned in US electrical-infrastructure equities, citing a private-equity holding (a generation-agnostic metal fabricator serving grid buildout) with order backlogs of three to five years - far longer than public grid-related companies (components of the PAVE and GRID ETFs) are willing to publicly disclose.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A private-market data point (multi-year backlogs) suggesting public grid-infrastructure companies may be understating their true revenue visibility, a potential re-rating catalyst.

insights.claim: Gromen favors Japanese industrial equities (distinct from AI-headline Japanese names) because US reshoring of manufacturing capacity is structurally dependent on Japanese capital-equipment expertise, with Korea and Germany able to help only 'at the margin' and China excluded for strategic reasons.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, still relatively early positioning idea (Japanese industrials over AI-hype names) tied to the broader US reindustrialization theme.

insights.claim: Rather than trying to call oil's direction directly, Gromen's personal and client positioning is to own gold, expecting it to outperform oil over time with lower volatility as the gold-to-oil ratio - recently compressed - normalizes back in gold's favor.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A concrete relative-value trade idea (long gold/oil ratio) distinct from a directional oil or gold call.

insights.claim: The Macro Voices 'trade of the week' buys GLD around $376 with a collar expiring September 18: downside protection effective from $370 to $350, financed by capping upside at $415 (about 10% above spot), for a net cost of about $1.75 per share ($175 per 100 shares) - a structure designed to lean bullish on gold after its roughly 30% six-month drawdown without needing to pick the exact bottom.
insights.speaker: Patrick, Macro Voices trading desk
insights.so_what: A fully specified, replicable options structure (strikes, expiration, net cost) for investors wanting asymmetric gold exposure with defined downside risk into a still-fragile technical setup.

insights.claim: CFTC COT data shows gold speculators (large and small) held their positioning essentially unchanged through gold's entire ~30% six-month drawdown, with large specs still holding nearly half the market and current positioning near the bottom of its one-year range - unusually 'sticky' positioning for that scale of correction.
insights.speaker: trading desk co-host, Macro Voices
insights.so_what: Sticky positioning through a large drawdown without capitulation suggests limited forced-selling risk remains in gold and potential fuel for a rally if sentiment turns.

insights.claim: S&P 500 and Dow COT data show both large and small speculators near the top decile (a positioning score around 90) of their one-year range, with small speculators adding nearly 30 points of positioning in a single week - a broadening of crowded bullish positioning that raises downside-volatility risk if a sell catalyst hits, with 7,400 flagged as the key S&P support level (a break risks a slide toward 7,000).
insights.speaker: trading desk co-host, Macro Voices
insights.so_what: Identifies both a specific crowding risk (broad-based bullish positioning) and a specific technical level (7,400 support, 7,000 downside target) for equity traders to watch into MAG7 earnings.

insights.claim: The US Dollar Index has broken out of a 15-month trading range with a bullish flag above its 50-day moving average (key level 101.50), EUR/USD is vulnerable below 1.14 toward 1.11-1.12, and USD/JPY has broken out to the 163 handle, while Canadian dollar speculative shorts sit at 48% of open interest - the most crowded, one-sided position across the entire COT report that week.
insights.speaker: Patrick, Macro Voices trading desk
insights.so_what: Flags a specific extreme (CAD shorts at 48% of open interest) as the most crowded FX trade currently on the board, a candidate for a violent short-covering move if sentiment shifts.

insights.claim: Crude oil rallied about 35% off its lows in three weeks back to the $90 handle (Brent near $100) on Iran re-escalation, but implied volatility (~65%) remains far below the ~120% seen in March, and WTI large speculators actually cut about 13,000 contracts into the rally (COT positioning score down to 12) - evidence the move is being driven by fundamentals/short-covering rather than fresh speculative buying.
insights.speaker: trading desk co-host, Macro Voices
insights.so_what: Specs selling into a strong rally with muted volatility suggests the oil market remains tight on fundamentals with a large sidelined pool of speculative buyers that hasn't chased the move yet.

insights.claim: Copper's May positioning extreme (large specs at a COT score of 100, holding about 29% of open interest) resolved through six weeks of sideways consolidation rather than a price correction, as falling Chinese inventories and rising import premiums kept physical demand strong even as speculative positioning cooled back to a score of about 75.
insights.speaker: trading desk co-host, Macro Voices
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration that crowded positioning is a 'condition, not a signal' - useful for avoiding premature contrarian shorts on other currently crowded trades.
